description: TERRASYNC CODE desarrolla una plataforma tecnológica de agricultura de precisión que integra observación terrestre de la NASA y arquitecturas de datos en SQLite para optimizar la rotación de cultivos . Buscamos transformar datos científicos complejos en decisiones prácticas para proteger los suelos, conservar recursos y fortalecer la resiliencia climática.
summary: TerraSync Code is an open-source agricultural decision-support web platform designed for arid and Andean valleys such as Moquegua, Peru—and extensible to any farm on Earth. By harmonizing NASA Earth observations (NASA POWER daily agroclimatology, SMAP L3 soil moisture, and Terra MODIS NDVI) with ISRIC SoilGrids properties and local crop parameters in a Python, SQLite, and interactive web architecture, the tool lets farmers and agronomists compare three crop rotation strategies side by side: baseline monoculture, nitrogen-fixing cover crops with inter-row habitat, and drought-tolerant deep-rooted rotations. It explicitly surfaces satellite resolution limits and data gaps to conserve water and build soil resilience without replacing local farming expertise.
details:
What it does & How it works: TerraSync Code ingests multi-resolution NASA agroclimatology (NASA POWER), surface soil moisture (SMAP L3), vegetation index (Terra MODIS NDVI), and soil property (ISRIC SoilGrids) datasets via Python scripts and stores harmonized time-series in a relational SQLite database. Through a bilingual (EN/ES) web interface, farmers and agronomists can explore four calibrated pilot valleys in Moquegua, Peru (Moquegua Valley, Samegua, Torata, and Omate) or click any farm coordinate on Earth for live API analysis. Users adjust water availability and management priorities to evaluate three rotation strategies side by side (current practice, nitrogen-fixing cover crops with inter-row habitat, and drought-tolerant deep-rooted alternatives), add field observations, and export CSV or printable reports.

Benefits & Expected Impact: By translating raw satellite observations into actionable local indicators (aridity index, Hargreaves-Samani reference evapotranspiration, and water stress index), the system helps farmers in arid and Andean valleys reduce irrigation demand, prevent soil degradation, and strengthen resilience against climate extremes.

Creativity & Factors Considered: Unlike complex GIS tools aimed at scientists, our approach focuses on farmer-centered transparency—explicitly surfacing spatial resolution mismatches (50 km climate grid vs. 9 km SMAP vs. 250 m NDVI/soil vs. smallholder plots), grid-cell elevation biases (such as the 3,851 m MERRA-2 mean), derived-estimate uncertainty, and local agronomic alerts (e.g., alkaline pH 8.1–8.2 constraints) so technology supports rather than replaces human expertise. We also accounted for water scarcity, market diversification, and offline/low-connectivity access.

Tools & Tech Stack: Python 3 (data ingestion, quality filtering, and spatial-temporal aggregation), SQLite (relational storage), HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, Leaflet.js (interactive mapping with Esri World Imagery), and Chart.js (time-series visualization).
